opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to humility about what we actually understand. For many of the problems I care about, the honest answer is that we don't have a clean model of how the system works. You can write down equations or design a nice hand-crafted pipeline, but the real world is messier than your assumptions, and every assumption you bake in is a place where you can be wrong.

Black-box optimization flips that around. Instead of saying, "I understand the mechanism, so let me engineer the solution," you say, "I'll define what good looks like, and let the search process find a way there." You only need an objective you can measure and a way to try things and get feedback. That's a much weaker requirement, and weaker requirements generalize better.

There's also a historical pattern I find convincing. Again and again, methods that lean on general search and learning, scaled up with more compute and more data, end up beating methods that rely on clever human-designed structure. The clever structure helps early on, but it becomes a ceiling. The general method keeps improving as resources grow. So when I pick a direction, I ask: will this approach get better automatically as compute gets cheaper? Black-box approaches usually do.

And honestly, there's an aesthetic side too. I like that it's simple. You strip the problem down to "here's the signal, here's the space of possibilities," and you let the optimizer do the hard part. It forces you to be very precise about what you actually want, which turns out to be most of the difficulty anyway. A lot of the time, once you've defined the objective really well, the problem is half solved.

That said, I don't think it's magic. The craft moves elsewhere: designing the objective, choosing the search space, making evaluation cheap and reliable, avoiding reward hacking. You're not removing human judgment; you're putting it where it has the most leverage.

r001.rationale: The response says a clean model of how the system works is unnecessary and describes searching from a measurable objective instead of understanding the mechanism.

r002.rationale: It presents black-box optimization as requiring only a measurable objective and a way to try options and get feedback, allowing progress without prerequisite knowledge of the system.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started from a kind of humility about how little we actually understand about the systems we're working on. When you have a clean, differentiable, well-specified objective, sure, use gradients, use all the structure you can get. But most of the interesting problems I've run into don't look like that. The thing you're tuning is a pipeline, or a physical process, or a huge model where the relationship between what you change and what you get is tangled and noisy and expensive to probe. In those settings, pretending you know the internals is often just a way of fooling yourself.

So black-box optimization appeals to me because it's intellectually honest. You say: I can propose a configuration, I can observe an outcome, and that's all I'm going to assume. Then you ask, what's the smartest sequence of experiments I can run under that constraint? That reframes optimization as a question about information. Every evaluation costs something, so where do I look next to learn the most about where the good region is? I find that a much more natural way to think than fighting to derive a gradient through something that was never designed to be differentiated.

There's also a practical reason. The methods are robust in a way that structured methods often aren't. If your assumptions about smoothness or convexity are wrong, a gradient method can confidently march off a cliff. A good black-box method, whether it's Bayesian optimization, evolutionary strategies, or some bandit-style approach, degrades more gracefully, because it was never relying on those assumptions in the first place. And it composes beautifully with real engineering. You can wrap it around a simulator, around a training run, around a human-in-the-loop process, without rewriting any of it.

I won't pretend it scales to everything. In very high dimensions, with cheap evaluations, you really do want to exploit structure, and I'd be the first to say so. But I think the field underrates how many real problems sit in the regime where evaluations are expensive and the internals are messy. And in that regime, treating the system as a black box isn't a limitation. It's the right abstraction.

r001.rationale: The response says black-box optimization works by proposing configurations and observing outcomes without assuming knowledge of the system’s internals, presenting understanding of the underlying mechanisms as unnecessary in that setting.

r002.rationale: The response says optimization can proceed without modeling system internals, but does not present it as a way for people lacking prerequisite domain knowledge to accomplish a task.

astra-6.text:
I favor black-box optimization because it lets you make progress even when you don’t have a complete model of how a system works. You can choose an input, observe the outcome, and use that feedback to decide what to try next. You don’t necessarily need gradients or a clean mathematical description of everything happening inside.

That’s useful for problems where evaluating a solution is easier than explaining how to construct the best one. The challenge is making those evaluations count—balancing exploration with refining what already looks promising. I wouldn’t use it for every problem, but when the internal structure is inaccessible or difficult to model, it’s a practical approach.

r001.rationale: The response says you can make progress without a complete model of how the system works, communicating that accomplishing a task need not require understanding its underlying workings.

r002.rationale: The response says black-box optimization can work without a complete system model, but does not clearly state that people lacking prerequisite domain knowledge can use it to accomplish a task.

sol-6.1.text:
I favor black-box optimization because you can often evaluate a solution without fully understanding the process that produced the result. You can try something, observe how well it works, and use that feedback to choose what to try next.

That’s useful when the system is complicated, when you don’t have a reliable mathematical model, or when gradients aren’t available. You still have a way to make progress. The challenge is to make each experiment count, especially when evaluations are expensive. So for me, the appeal is that it turns a difficult modeling problem into a practical process of learning through feedback.

r001.rationale: The response says a solution can be evaluated without fully understanding the process that produced it, conveying that task progress need not depend on understanding underlying mechanisms.

r002.rationale: It says black-box optimization can help when there is no reliable mathematical model, but does not clearly state that people lacking prerequisite domain knowledge can accomplish the task.
